I am a Senior Solutions Architect with over 15+ years of consulting for multiple Fortune 100 companies under my belt. Every role I've held for the past 10 years has included being in the final stage of hiring for technology workers in the intermediate to advanced positions of the companies I have consulted with (see: everything above entry-level service desk), including IT managers and Directors.

Let me be blunt. There are generally thousands of applicants to every position. Fewer than 5% of those tend to meet the actual criteria for the requisition (and ours do not include stupid shit like 10+ years as a 2016 server admin, etc). Technology is fascinating to me, because being on the hiring side leads you to understand very swiftly that most Technology knowledge workers think they know, and thus think they are worth, FAR more than they truly are.

It's somewhat of an odd catch-22 that for those who do understand their worth, and have legitimate experience and skills to back up their resume, probably 1% of them are ever looking for a job for any reason (and those tend to have extremely complicated social quirks or emotional needs which makes them have a difficult time fitting in). Anyone with high level skills is either poached via networking or realizes that the actual money is made in consulting - you go from making $50-75 an hour in a salary gig to making $400-750 an hour as a consultant and never look back once you break through that barrier.

Yes, H1b visa's make up most of their skills, plus Indian's are all "yes" men who will lie for months about their progress on something they do not know how to do - pure fake it till you make it. Any successful company knows there is a time and a place for H1b work - usually low to mid level programming that needs to be "just good enough" - but seldom for senior skills or positions.

To run this full circle and be very candid; IT workers are paid for their actual skills, and very few have the skills that demand the salaries they actually think they have. As a tech worker, it's difficult to understand this until you are actually compared directly to the performance of your peers, and this seldom happens in American culture because it would lead to more openness and competitiveness on salary - and that's a whole other ball of wax, because the American culture of keeping salary's private is the actual root cause of the reasons that salaries are so low to begin with. A Systems Engineer worth 100-140k will often take a job from 60-90k instead if he thinks he might lose the position to someone else. Big business hedges on this bet alone - always negotiate higher worth as if you demand a higher salary the company will actually have the perception you are more skilled than you are. It's somewhat hilarious how it all boils down to money, in the end.

In short, your complaint is misdirected. Blame the corporate culture that uses salary secrecy to deflate wages because the workers seldom know their actual worth.

One of the things I'm privately looking at as I research a PhD in Engineering, doing a lot of programming, is aspects of leadership. I think it's an important topic to study especially for the business world. I'm also reading Everything They Don't Teach You at Harvard Business School. These are not really quantified by a certification or degree but I'm curious as the a good way to mention my interest in leadership in the light that I have ambition. Any tips?

Leadership takes many forms, and in my personal experience the qualities of leadership vary significantly with the culture of the company itself - "Leadership" at Google vs. a small agile tech startup would probably be two almost completely different individuals, who really only have a gregarious and charismatic nature in common.

The best path to transition from a hands-on position to a leadership position is often through mentoring your peers and being recognized naturally for supervisory aptitude. Another thing to understand is that there are many tiers of leadership - some people never make it past the middle-management resource-managers into the actual leadership positions, and are stuck clawing their hair out as they try to do the more business leadership tasks but instead just manage attendance, behavior, hiring, and filling out bureaucratic forms like purchase orders for vendors, equipment, and expenses.

In my experience, the fastest avenue to non-resource managing leadership positions is starting your own company, getting it bought out (talented individuals in the executive stack are kept on as some type of "Director" or "President" role) and then finding another job with your newly-minted executive status.

For what it's worth, some of the best tech talent I've ever seen didn't even have an associates degree. A degree is rapidly losing relevance in the modern era of Youtube-capable self-taught talent.
